seoTitle: Cash-on-cash return Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: Cash-on-cash return: work out effective gross income from the gross annual rental income and the vacancy rate. A free finance calculator with the formula,…
summary: effective gross income is what the Cash-on-cash return calculator works out, and it gets there from the gross annual rental income, the vacancy rate, the cash-on-cash return and the net operating income. That makes it useful for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Cash-on-cash return calculator work?
sections.html:
The Cash-on-cash return calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports effective gross income in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the gross annual rental income (100% occupancy), the vacancy rate, the cash-on-cash return and the net operating income.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Cash-on-cash return calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Effective gross income=gross annual rental income (100% occupancy) × (1 − vacancy rate)
Monthly loan payment=(1 ÷ 12) × annual debt service
Effective gross income=annual expenses for this property + net operating income
Annual cash flow=-annual debt service + net operating income
Total cash investment=annual cash flow ÷ cash-on-cash return

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Gross annual rental income (100% occupancy) = 10 and Vacancy rate = 10 %. Working through the relationship above gives Effective gross income = 9.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Effective gross income = 9 should be roughly the size you expected from Gross annual rental income (100% occupancy) = 10 and Vacancy rate = 10 %.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Cash-on-cash return calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the gross annual rental income, the vacancy rate and the cash-on-cash return — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Cash-on-cash return calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns effective gross income, derived from the gross annual rental income, the vacancy rate and the cash-on-cash return. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Cash-on-cash return calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the gross annual rental income, the vacancy rate, the cash-on-cash return and the net operating income, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter total cash investment in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Total cash investment opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Effective gross income = 9. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Cash-on-cash return calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
